clue.text: Novel result of traffic-light malfunction?

parts.note: a jammed signal would stay at its middle colour for all time, which also names a famous 1944 romance novel by Kathleen Winsor

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what a broken set of traffic lights might lead to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new; it is the noun, a book title.
explanation.definitionFit: Kathleen Winsor's bestselling historical romance carries this title, and a stuck light would show yellow endlessly.

clue.text: Anticipated number reportedly observed

indicators.note: reportedly tells us a word is to be heard rather than spelt as written

parts.note: four is a number
observed means saw

explanation.surface: A predicted figure was, so people say, actually seen.
explanation.definitionFit: To have foreseen something is to have anticipated it, a synonym in the past tense.

clue.text: Work of poet audience might think is Frost?

indicators.note: listeners hearing the word could take it for a different spelling, so this marks a sound-alike

parts.note: rime is hoar frost

explanation.surface: A listener mistakes a poem for the work of Robert Frost.
explanation.walkthrough: Frost with its capital suggests the American poet Robert Frost; here it is just icy rime.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse that chimes at line ends is a poet's product, so the poem itself is the poet's work.

clue.text: Card from Italian gentleman

definitions.meaning: a greeting card sent on 14 February
One of Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona

explanation.definitionFit: A love card sent each February bears the name, and Shakespeare's Verona comedy has a gentleman so called.

clue.text: Best rating in the navy? That's right, they say

indicators.note: in places the top grade inside the letters for the navy

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy
A1 (written AI) is the best rating, as in Lloyd's Register of ships

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the top grade in the fleet is right, and is told it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' suggests a sailor, a naval rating; it is a grade. The definition leans on the saying 'right as rain', meaning perfectly fine.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'right as rain' pairs the word with being correct or perfectly well, so the saying links them.

clue.text: A case abandoned in the wind I found

indicators.note: in tells us the letter I sits within the wind's name

parts.note: the mistral is the cold north wind of southern France

explanation.surface: Someone reports finding a suitcase blown away in a gale.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial ended without verdict, through error or a hung jury, is a legal case abandoned.

clue.text: Bet he'll avoid extremes for her

indicators.note: dropping the very first and very last letters of the phrase Bet he'll leaves its inner run

explanation.surface: A gambler is sure some man will play it safe for a woman's sake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoid extremes' strips the first and last letters, B and L, from BETHELL, leaving the run inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so a fair stand-in for a female pronoun.

clue.text: Conservative group prior to change in Whitehall

definitions.meaning: the long-standing, traditionalist members of a party or body
the outgoing sentries before the Changing of the Guard at Horse Guards in Whitehall, London

explanation.surface: A traditionalist faction waits before reforms in British government.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitehall suggests the civil service, but here it is the London street where the Horse Guards sentries are relieved in a daily ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditionalist stalwarts resisting reform are called this, and literally it is the sentry detail before relief.

clue.text: Look carefully for American poet

parts.note: lo is an old word for look
well means carefully, as in done well

explanation.surface: Readers are told to search closely for a US writer of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert and Amy of that surname, and James Russell too, were noted American writers of verse.

clue.text: Reward for author with connexions at court

definitions.meaning: payments made to a writer on each copy sold

explanation.surface: A writer is paid for having links with the royal household.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers earn a percentage per copy sold under this name, and royal personages collectively share it.

clue.text: Greeting first two characters from tragedy

indicators.note: the opening pair of letters is to be removed from the play's title

parts.note: Othello is a Shakespeare tragedy

explanation.surface: Actors greet the first two characters to appear in a tragic play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests people in the play; they are letters, and 'from' means taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: A word said when meeting someone, the commonest salutation.

clue.text: Behind a lot of bones

parts.note: the stern is the back part of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone is lagging behind a large heap of bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' reads as one phrase, but A belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of sternum, the breastbone, so several such bones together.

clue.text: Introduction for you, say, in a theatre box

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: in puts the letter for you inside the theatre box

parts.note: a loge is a box in a theatre

indicators.note: say marks a letter that sounds like the word you

parts.note: the word heard aloud as the letter U

explanation.surface: Someone is offered an opening speech while sitting in a theatre box.
explanation.definitionFit: An opening speech before a play, an introductory section.

clue.text: Small, nasty, tailless, beetle

parts.note: wee is Scots for small

indicators.note: without its last letter, the tail of the word for nasty

parts.note: vile means nasty

explanation.surface: A tiny unpleasant beetle that has lost its tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A snout beetle, a grain and crop pest of the family Curculionidae.

clue.text: He assesses what's written in the papers

definitions.text: He assesses what's written in the papers

parts.words: He assesses what's written in the papers
parts.note: reads like a press critic judging newspaper articles, but means one marking candidates' exam scripts

explanation.surface: A man reviews what the newspapers have published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests newspapers; it means exam papers.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who marks candidates' scripts in a test judges what they have written.

clue.text: Babe's recollected by everybody for this

definitions.text: Babe's recollected by everybody for this

indicators.note: recollected read as re-collected, gathered up again in a new order

parts.note: the letters of Babe's, the apostrophe ignored
all means everybody

explanation.surface: Babe Ruth is remembered by everyone for his sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recollected' means remembered on the surface but re-collected, rearranged, in the wordplay: BASEB from BABES, then ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Babe Ruth, the American slugger, is remembered for this bat-and-ball game.

clue.text: Naturally nobody speaks this form of neat prose

indicators.note: a new form of the letters of neat prose, rearranged

explanation.surface: A tidy style of writing that no one would talk in.
explanation.walkthrough: An invented language has no native speakers, so 'naturally nobody speaks' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Zamenhof's constructed international language has almost no native speakers.

clue.text: Grace's approval

definitions.meaning: a short prayer said before a meal
sanction or consent, as in giving your support

explanation.definitionFit: A prayer asking divine favour on a meal, and also consent, as in giving a plan your support.

clue.text: Money doubled by a girl I found in Wales

parts.note: L stands for pound, from Latin libra
doubled gives the pound sign a second time
Nell is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Two pounds go with a young woman I met somewhere in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in Carmarthenshire, south-west Wales.

clue.text: To create a ferment, go South?

definitions.meaning: to raise dough with yeast, or to stir things up
to quit the north, ..., is to head the other way

explanation.definitionFit: To raise dough with yeast; cryptically, quitting the north (leave N) means heading for the south.

clue.text: Model of perseverance wretched king spied

indicators.note: wretched suggests the word spied has been battered out of shape

parts.note: R is short for rex, king

explanation.surface: A miserable monarch saw the creature that taught him to keep trying.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says Robert the Bruce, a Scottish king, hiding in a cave, took heart from one that kept trying to spin its web.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert the Bruce's cave-dwelling arachnid became the legendary emblem of trying again and again.

clue.text: Building seen, in grand' tour, perhaps-not Greek

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of grand tour might be arranged some other way
not tells us the letters for Greek are left out of the rearranged pool

explanation.surface: A sight on the classic European cultural trip, though maybe not a Greek one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges GRANDTOUR and 'not' takes out the G and R that stand for Greek. The Grand Tour was a young gentleman's educational trip round Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: A round domed hall or structure, like the Pantheon in Rome.

clue.text: Dictates letters for crucial trial

indicators.note: only the word's letters are used, taken in a new order

explanation.surface: A ruler issues orders in writing for a decisive test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' looks like correspondence; it says the letters of Dictates are reused.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally the nitric acid assay for gold, now any decisive test.

clue.text: Plant 2 for 2

indicators.note: for marks a swap, one letter standing in place of another

parts.note: the answer to clue 2-down
Tea for Two: T is read as standing for two

explanation.surface: A puzzle shorthand: one plant entered for another.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 2 is T, punning on the song 'Tea for Two'; the second is the answer to 2-down, whose R is swapped out.
explanation.definitionFit: A small aromatic herb of the mint family used in cooking.

clue.text: Mainly loyal worker is absentee

indicators.note: mainly means most of the word, its last letter dropped

parts.note: true means loyal
an ant is a worker insect

explanation.surface: A largely faithful employee turns out to be missing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil who skips school without leave is an absentee.

clue.text: Quick article, as it happens

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
a live broadcast goes out as it happens

explanation.surface: A fast news story, reported in real time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' means living, as in 'the quick and the dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old sense, the quick are the living, as in the Bible's 'the quick and the dead'.

clue.text: Test part that's finished

definitions.meaning: a set of six balls in a cricket Test match

explanation.definitionFit: A cricket Test match is made of six-ball sets, and the same word means ended.

clue.text: Satan's other side

definitions.meaning: the Devil, often called the arch-foe of mankind
the opposing force in a war or contest

explanation.definitionFit: The Devil is traditionally called the Foe of mankind, and in war the other side is the foe.

clue.text: Story — one of many written by Kipling

definitions.text: one of many written by Kipling
definitions.meaning: Many ... is an 1893 collection of Kipling stories

explanation.definitionFit: A fabrication is a made-up tale, and Kipling's 1893 collection was titled Many Inventions.

clue.text: Gay entertainment, not for the choosy?

definitions.text: Gay entertainment, not for the choosy?

parts.words: Gay entertainment, not for the choosy?
parts.note: John Gay's 1728 ballad opera, with the proverb that those who ask for charity cannot be choosers

explanation.surface: A cheerful show that fussy people should avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay' looks like an adjective meaning merry; it is John Gay, the 18th-century writer.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gay's 1728 ballad opera about thieves and highwaymen; the proverb says those asking for alms cannot be choosers.
